questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Let A be NP-complete and let B ∈ P. Which of the following is TRUE?
options: A ≤p B
both A ≤p B and B ≤p A
neither reduction exists
B ≤p A

solution.concept: An NP-hard target accepts a reduction from every NP language, and P ⊆ NP, so every problem in P reduces to A. The reverse reduction would collapse P and NP.
steps: Since B ∈ P and P ⊆ NP, B is a language in NP.
A is NP-complete, hence NP-hard, so every language in NP reduces to A; in particular B ≤p A.
If A ≤p B also held, then A would lie in P by the easiness-transfer property, and since A is NP-hard that would give P = NP.
P = NP is not known, so A ≤p B is not a theorem and option B fails.
Option C fails because B ≤p A does exist.
solution.trap: Assuming reducibility is symmetric because both problems are 'polynomial-time related'. ≤p is a preorder, not an equivalence: the direction carries all the meaning.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An NP-hard target accepts a reduction from every NP language, and P ⊆ NP, so every problem in P reduces to A. The reverse reduction would collapse P and NP.

Step by step.

  1. Since B ∈ P and P ⊆ NP, B is a language in NP.
  2. A is NP-complete, hence NP-hard, so every language in NP reduces to A; in particular B ≤p A.
  3. If A ≤p B also held, then A would lie in P by the easiness-transfer property, and since A is NP-hard that would give P = NP.
  4. P = NP is not known, so A ≤p B is not a theorem and option B fails.
  5. Option C fails because B ≤p A does exist.

Answer: B ≤p A — option D.

Common misconception. Assuming reducibility is symmetric because both problems are 'polynomial-time related'. ≤p is a preorder, not an equivalence: the direction carries all the meaning.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which problem was the first to be proved NP-complete?
options: SAT, in the Cook–Levin theorem
3-SAT
CLIQUE
HAMILTONIAN CYCLE

solution.concept: Cook and Levin showed in 1971 that Boolean satisfiability is NP-complete, giving the first member of the class and therefore a root for all later reductions.
steps: The proof encodes the entire computation of a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine as a Boolean formula.
The formula is satisfiable exactly when the machine has an accepting computation, and its size is polynomial in the input length.
That makes SAT NP-hard, and SAT is in NP because an assignment is a polynomial certificate.
Every later NP-completeness result reduces from SAT or from one of its descendants.
3-SAT, CLIQUE and HAMILTONIAN CYCLE came afterwards, each by reduction.
solution.trap: Answering 3-SAT because it is the more convenient starting point for later reductions. 3-SAT is derived from SAT by a reduction that splits long clauses.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Cook and Levin showed in 1971 that Boolean satisfiability is NP-complete, giving the first member of the class and therefore a root for all later reductions.

Step by step.

  1. The proof encodes the entire computation of a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine as a Boolean formula.
  2. The formula is satisfiable exactly when the machine has an accepting computation, and its size is polynomial in the input length.
  3. That makes SAT NP-hard, and SAT is in NP because an assignment is a polynomial certificate.
  4. Every later NP-completeness result reduces from SAT or from one of its descendants.
  5. 3-SAT, CLIQUE and HAMILTONIAN CYCLE came afterwards, each by reduction.

Answer: SAT — option A.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following problems is NP-complete?
options: 2-SAT
deciding whether a graph has an Eulerian circuit
HAMILTONIAN CYCLE
single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights

solution.concept: The Hamiltonian and Eulerian conditions are the standard contrast: visiting every vertex once is hard, traversing every edge once is easy.
steps: A: 2-SAT is decided in linear time through strongly connected components of the implication graph, so it is in P.
B: a connected graph has an Eulerian circuit exactly when every vertex has even degree, which is checked in linear time.
C: HAMILTONIAN CYCLE is NP-complete, by reduction from VERTEX COVER; no polynomial algorithm is known.
D: Dijkstra's algorithm solves it in O(E + V log V) time with non-negative weights.
So only option C is NP-complete.
solution.trap: Confusing Eulerian with Hamiltonian. 'Every edge exactly once' is a degree condition; 'every vertex exactly once' is the hard one.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The Hamiltonian and Eulerian conditions are the standard contrast: visiting every vertex once is hard, traversing every edge once is easy.

Step by step.

  2. B: a connected graph has an Eulerian circuit exactly when every vertex has even degree, which is checked in linear time.
  3. C: HAMILTONIAN CYCLE is NP-complete, by reduction from VERTEX COVER; no polynomial algorithm is known.
  4. D: Dijkstra's algorithm solves it in O(E + V log V) time with non-negative weights.
  5. So only option C is NP-complete.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: If any NP-complete language belongs to P then P = NP.
Every language in NP is polynomial-time reducible to every NP-complete language.
There are infinitely many NP-complete languages.
The complement of an NP-complete language is NP-complete.

solution.concept: NP-completeness is defined by being both in NP and NP-hard, and its consequences follow from the transitivity of ≤p.
steps: A: an NP-complete language is NP-hard, so every language of NP reduces to it; if it were in P, every language of NP would be in P. TRUE.
B: that is precisely the NP-hard half of the definition of NP-complete. TRUE.
C: from one NP-complete language infinitely many are obtained, for example by padding or by intersecting with trivially different regular sets, all still NP-complete. TRUE.
D: the complement of an NP-complete language is co-NP-complete; if it were NP-complete then NP = co-NP, which is open. FALSE.
solution.final: Options (A), (B) and (C) are TRUE; (D) is not.
solution.trap: Assuming NP-completeness is inherited by the complement. It is inherited by co-NP-completeness, and identifying the two classes is exactly the open NP versus co-NP question.

Step by step.

  1. A: an NP-complete language is NP-hard, so every language of NP reduces to it; if it were in P, every language of NP would be in P. TRUE.
  2. B: that is precisely the NP-hard half of the definition of NP-complete. TRUE.
  3. C: from one NP-complete language infinitely many are obtained, for example by padding or by intersecting with trivially different regular sets, all still NP-complete. TRUE.
  4. D: the complement of an NP-complete language is co-NP-complete; if it were NP-complete then NP = co-NP, which is open. FALSE.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: A graph G has n = 10 vertices. The reduction CLIQUE ≤p VERTEX-COVER replaces G by its complement and sets the required cover size to n − k. G has a clique of size 4 exactly when its complement has a vertex cover of size:

solution.concept: A clique in G is an independent set in the complement, and the complement of a maximum independent set is a minimum vertex cover.
steps: A set S is a clique in G exactly when no two of its vertices are non-adjacent in G, that is, exactly when S is an independent set in the complement graph.
In any graph, S is an independent set exactly when V − S is a vertex cover: every edge has at least one end outside S.
So a clique of size k in G corresponds to an independent set of size k in the complement, and hence to a vertex cover of size n − k there.
With n = 10 and k = 4, the cover size is 10 − 4 = 6.
solution.trap: Answering 4 by keeping the same size, or 14 by adding instead of subtracting. The correspondence is a complement of the vertex set, so the sizes sum to n.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A clique in G is an independent set in the complement, and the complement of a maximum independent set is a minimum vertex cover.

Step by step.

  1. A set S is a clique in G exactly when no two of its vertices are non-adjacent in G, that is, exactly when S is an independent set in the complement graph.
  2. In any graph, S is an independent set exactly when V − S is a vertex cover: every edge has at least one end outside S.
  3. So a clique of size k in G corresponds to an independent set of size k in the complement, and hence to a vertex cover of size n − k there.
  4. With n = 10 and k = 4, the cover size is 10 − 4 = 6.

Answer: 6 — option B.

Common misconception. Answering 4 by keeping the same size, or 14 by adding instead of subtracting. The correspondence is a complement of the vertex set, so the sizes sum to n.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Apply the standard reduction from 3-SAT to CLIQUE to φ = (x₁ ∨ x₂ ∨ ¬x₃) ∧ (¬x₁ ∨ x₂ ∨ x₃) ∧ (x₁ ∨ ¬x₂ ∨ x₃) ∧ (¬x₁ ∨ ¬x₂ ∨ ¬x₃). One vertex is created for each literal occurrence, and an edge joins two vertices that lie in different clauses when their literals are not complementary. How many edges does the constructed graph have?

solution.concept: The reduction builds a vertex per literal occurrence and joins every cross-clause pair except the contradictory ones, so the edge count is the number of cross-clause pairs minus the number of complementary pairs.
steps: Four clauses of three literals give 4 × 3 = 12 vertices.
Pairs inside one clause are never joined: 4 × C(3,2) = 12 of them, leaving C(12,2) − 12 = 66 − 12 = 54 cross-clause pairs.

Count the complementary pairs, clause pair by clause pair: clauses 1 and 2 give (x₁, ¬x₁) and (¬x₃, x₃); clauses 1 and 3 give (x₂, ¬x₂) and (¬x₃, x₃); clauses 1 and 4 give (x₁, ¬x₁) and (x₂, ¬x₂); clauses 2 and 3 give (¬x₁, x₁) and (x₂, ¬x₂); clauses 2 and 4 give (x₂, ¬x₂) and (x₃, ¬x₃); clauses 3 and 4 give (x₁, ¬x₁) and (x₃, ¬x₃).
That is 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 12 complementary pairs, each excluded.
Edges = 54 − 12 = 42.
solution.trap: Forgetting to subtract the within-clause pairs (giving 54), or subtracting only one complementary pair per clause pair (giving 48). Every literal has exactly one complement among the twelve, and the count above pairs them all.

Detailed solution

Concept. The reduction builds a vertex per literal occurrence and joins every cross-clause pair except the contradictory ones, so the edge count is the number of cross-clause pairs minus the number of complementary pairs.

Step by step.

  1. Four clauses of three literals give 4 × 3 = 12 vertices.
  2. Pairs inside one clause are never joined: 4 × C(3,2) = 12 of them, leaving C(12,2) − 12 = 66 − 12 = 54 cross-clause pairs.
  3. Count the complementary pairs, clause pair by clause pair: clauses 1 and 2 give (x₁, ¬x₁) and (¬x₃, x₃); clauses 1 and 3 give (x₂, ¬x₂) and (¬x₃, x₃); clauses 1 and 4 give (x₁, ¬x₁) and (x₂, ¬x₂); clauses 2 and 3 give (¬x₁, x₁) and (x₂, ¬x₂); clauses 2 and 4 give (x₂, ¬x₂) and (x₃, ¬x₃); clauses 3 and 4 give (x₁, ¬x₁) and (x₃, ¬x₃).
  4. That is 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 12 complementary pairs, each excluded.
  5. Edges = 54 − 12 = 42.

Answer: 42 edges.

Common misconception. Forgetting to subtract the within-clause pairs (giving 54), or subtracting only one complementary pair per clause pair (giving 48). Every literal has exactly one complement among the twelve, and the count above pairs them all.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: 3-SAT and HAMILTONIAN CYCLE are both NP-complete. Which of the following is TRUE?
options: 3-SAT ≤p HAMILTONIAN CYCLE, but not conversely
neither problem reduces to the other
HAMILTONIAN CYCLE ≤p 3-SAT, but not conversely
each problem reduces to the other in polynomial time

solution.concept: All NP-complete problems are mutually reducible: each is NP-hard, so each reduces to every other member of NP.
steps: 3-SAT is NP-complete, hence NP-hard, and HAMILTONIAN CYCLE lies in NP, so HAMILTONIAN CYCLE ≤p 3-SAT.
By the same argument with the roles exchanged, 3-SAT ≤p HAMILTONIAN CYCLE.
Both directions hold simultaneously; there is no asymmetry among NP-complete problems.
Reducibility is a preorder, so the two problems sit in one equivalence class under mutual reduction.
solution.final: Each reduces to the other — option D.
solution.trap: Believing one NP-complete problem is 'more fundamental' than another because SAT came first historically. Historical order affects proofs, not reducibility.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. All NP-complete problems are mutually reducible: each is NP-hard, so each reduces to every other member of NP.

Step by step.

  1. 3-SAT is NP-complete, hence NP-hard, and HAMILTONIAN CYCLE lies in NP, so HAMILTONIAN CYCLE ≤p 3-SAT.
  2. By the same argument with the roles exchanged, 3-SAT ≤p HAMILTONIAN CYCLE.
  3. Both directions hold simultaneously; there is no asymmetry among NP-complete problems.
  4. Reducibility is a preorder, so the two problems sit in one equivalence class under mutual reduction.

Answer: Each reduces to the other — option D.

Common misconception. Believing one NP-complete problem is 'more fundamental' than another because SAT came first historically. Historical order affects proofs, not reducibility.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: How does NP-hard differ from NP-complete?
options: An NP-hard problem must lie in NP, whereas an NP-complete problem need not.
An NP-hard problem need not lie in NP and may even be undecidable, whereas NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP.
The two terms are synonyms.
NP-hard problems are exactly those with no polynomial-time algorithm, whereas NP-complete problems have one.

solution.concept: NP-complete = NP-hard ∩ NP. Hardness alone says every NP language reduces to the problem; it says nothing about whether the problem's own solutions can be checked quickly.
steps: NP-hardness is a lower bound: every language in NP reduces to the problem in polynomial time.
That definition never mentions membership in NP, so a problem outside NP can be NP-hard.
The halting problem is the standard example: it is NP-hard because SAT reduces to it, yet it is undecidable and therefore not in NP.
Adding the requirement of membership in NP gives NP-completeness.
Option D confuses the definition with a consequence: hardness means no polynomial algorithm unless P = NP, but the converse does not define the class.
solution.final: NP-hard need not be in NP — option B.
solution.trap: Using the two names interchangeably. Every NP-complete problem is NP-hard, but the halting problem is NP-hard and not NP-complete.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. NP-complete = NP-hard ∩ NP. Hardness alone says every NP language reduces to the problem; it says nothing about whether the problem's own solutions can be checked quickly.

Step by step.

  1. NP-hardness is a lower bound: every language in NP reduces to the problem in polynomial time.
  2. That definition never mentions membership in NP, so a problem outside NP can be NP-hard.
  3. The halting problem is the standard example: it is NP-hard because SAT reduces to it, yet it is undecidable and therefore not in NP.
  4. Adding the requirement of membership in NP gives NP-completeness.
  5. Option D confuses the definition with a consequence: hardness means no polynomial algorithm unless P = NP, but the converse does not define the class.

Answer: NP-hard need not be in NP — option B.

Common misconception. Using the two names interchangeably. Every NP-complete problem is NP-hard, but the halting problem is NP-hard and not NP-complete.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following problems are NP-hard? (Select all that apply.)
options: 2-SAT
the halting problem
deciding whether a given DFA accepts every string
the travelling-salesman optimisation problem, that is, finding a minimum-cost tour

solution.concept: NP-hardness is about being at least as hard as everything in NP; it is not restricted to problems inside NP, nor granted to problems that turn out to be in P.
steps: A: 2-SAT is in P, so it is NP-hard only if P = NP; it is not known to be NP-hard. Not selected.
B: SAT reduces to the halting problem, so every language of NP reduces to it; it is NP-hard, and undecidable. Selected.
C: DFA universality is decided by a product construction in polynomial time, so it is in P and not known to be NP-hard. Not selected.
D: the optimisation form of TSP is at least as hard as its NP-complete decision form, so it is NP-hard; it is not in NP because it is not a decision problem. Selected.
solution.trap: Restricting NP-hard to problems in NP, which would exclude both the halting problem and the TSP optimisation problem. Hardness is a lower bound and applies outside NP.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. NP-hardness is about being at least as hard as everything in NP; it is not restricted to problems inside NP, nor granted to problems that turn out to be in P.

Step by step.

  1. A: 2-SAT is in P, so it is NP-hard only if P = NP; it is not known to be NP-hard. Not selected.
  2. B: SAT reduces to the halting problem, so every language of NP reduces to it; it is NP-hard, and undecidable. Selected.
  3. C: DFA universality is decided by a product construction in polynomial time, so it is in P and not known to be NP-hard. Not selected.
  4. D: the optimisation form of TSP is at least as hard as its NP-complete decision form, so it is NP-hard; it is not in NP because it is not a decision problem. Selected.

Answer: Options (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Restricting NP-hard to problems in NP, which would exclude both the halting problem and the TSP optimisation problem. Hardness is a lower bound and applies outside NP.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: The optimisation version of the travelling-salesman problem, which asks for a minimum-cost tour, is:
options: NP-hard, and not known to belong to NP
NP-complete
in P
undecidable

solution.concept: NP contains decision problems only. An optimisation problem can be NP-hard without being a member of NP, because there is no yes/no answer to certify.
steps: The decision form — is there a tour of cost at most k — is NP-complete.
Any algorithm for the optimisation form yields an algorithm for the decision form by comparing the optimum with k, so the optimisation form is at least as hard, hence NP-hard.
Membership in NP requires a language, that is a set of strings with a yes/no answer; a minimum-cost tour is a function value, not a decision.
So the optimisation form is NP-hard but is not a member of NP, and therefore not NP-complete.
It is decidable, since enumerating all tours terminates, so it is not undecidable either.
solution.final: NP-hard, and not known to be in NP — option A.
solution.trap: Calling every NP-hard problem NP-complete. The optimisation form fails the membership half of the definition.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. NP contains decision problems only. An optimisation problem can be NP-hard without being a member of NP, because there is no yes/no answer to certify.

Step by step.

  1. The decision form — is there a tour of cost at most k — is NP-complete.
  2. Any algorithm for the optimisation form yields an algorithm for the decision form by comparing the optimum with k, so the optimisation form is at least as hard, hence NP-hard.
  3. Membership in NP requires a language, that is a set of strings with a yes/no answer; a minimum-cost tour is a function value, not a decision.
  4. So the optimisation form is NP-hard but is not a member of NP, and therefore not NP-complete.
  5. It is decidable, since enumerating all tours terminates, so it is not undecidable either.

Answer: NP-hard, and not known to be in NP — option A.

Common misconception. Calling every NP-hard problem NP-complete. The optimisation form fails the membership half of the definition.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Among the four decision problems 3-SAT, 2-SAT, CLIQUE and single-source shortest paths, how many are NP-complete?

solution.concept: Separating the NP-complete members of a short list from their polynomial-time look-alikes.
steps: 3-SAT is NP-complete: it is in NP, and SAT reduces to it.
2-SAT is in P, decided in linear time by strongly connected components of the implication graph.
CLIQUE is NP-complete, by reduction from 3-SAT.
Single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights is in P by Dijkstra's algorithm.
The NP-complete members are 3-SAT and CLIQUE, so the count is 2.
solution.trap: Counting 2-SAT because it shares the word 'SAT'. The two-literal restriction removes the hardness entirely.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Separating the NP-complete members of a short list from their polynomial-time look-alikes.

Step by step.

  1. 3-SAT is NP-complete: it is in NP, and SAT reduces to it.
  2. 2-SAT is in P, decided in linear time by strongly connected components of the implication graph.
  3. CLIQUE is NP-complete, by reduction from 3-SAT.
  4. Single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights is in P by Dijkstra's algorithm.
  5. The NP-complete members are 3-SAT and CLIQUE, so the count is 2.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Counting 2-SAT because it shares the word 'SAT'. The two-literal restriction removes the hardness entirely.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Suppose L is NP-hard and L ≤p L′. Which of the following follows?
options: L′ must belong to NP.
L′ must be NP-complete.
L′ must be NP-hard.
nothing follows about L′.

solution.concept: Hardness travels forward along a reduction: if everything in NP reaches L, and L reaches L′, then everything in NP reaches L′.
steps: Let A ∈ NP. Since L is NP-hard, A ≤p L.
We are given L ≤p L′, so by transitivity A ≤p L′.
This holds for every A ∈ NP, which is exactly the statement that L′ is NP-hard.
Nothing is claimed about membership: L′ may lie outside NP, so option A and option B both fail.
Option D fails because the conclusion in option C does follow.
solution.final: L′ must be NP-hard — option C.
solution.trap: Concluding NP-completeness, which needs the extra fact L′ ∈ NP. Hardness alone is preserved by the reduction; membership is not.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Hardness travels forward along a reduction: if everything in NP reaches L, and L reaches L′, then everything in NP reaches L′.

Step by step.

  1. Let A ∈ NP. Since L is NP-hard, A ≤p L.
  2. We are given L ≤p L′, so by transitivity A ≤p L′.
  3. This holds for every A ∈ NP, which is exactly the statement that L′ is NP-hard.
  4. Nothing is claimed about membership: L′ may lie outside NP, so option A and option B both fail.
  5. Option D fails because the conclusion in option C does follow.

Answer: L′ must be NP-hard — option C.

Common misconception. Concluding NP-completeness, which needs the extra fact L′ ∈ NP. Hardness alone is preserved by the reduction; membership is not.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Consider six problems: (i) the halting problem, (ii) the decision version of the travelling-salesman problem, (iii) 2-SAT, (iv) SAT, (v) deciding whether a given DFA accepts every string, (vi) VERTEX COVER. How many of the six are NP-hard?

solution.concept: NP-hard covers the NP-complete problems plus everything above them, including undecidable problems; only problems known to be in P are excluded.
steps: (i) The halting problem is undecidable, and SAT reduces to it, so it is NP-hard.
(ii) The decision form of TSP is NP-complete, hence NP-hard.
(iii) 2-SAT is in P, so it is NP-hard only if P = NP; it is not counted.
(iv) SAT is NP-complete, hence NP-hard.
(v) DFA universality is decided in polynomial time by a product construction, so it is not counted.
(vi) VERTEX COVER is NP-complete, hence NP-hard.
The NP-hard problems are (i), (ii), (iv) and (vi), four in all.
solution.trap: Excluding the halting problem because it is undecidable, or including 2-SAT because it looks like SAT. Hardness is a lower bound and reaches beyond NP, while polynomial-time problems are below it.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. NP-hard covers the NP-complete problems plus everything above them, including undecidable problems; only problems known to be in P are excluded.

Step by step.

  1. (i) The halting problem is undecidable, and SAT reduces to it, so it is NP-hard.
  2. (ii) The decision form of TSP is NP-complete, hence NP-hard.
  3. (iii) 2-SAT is in P, so it is NP-hard only if P = NP; it is not counted.
  4. (iv) SAT is NP-complete, hence NP-hard.
  5. (v) DFA universality is decided in polynomial time by a product construction, so it is not counted.
  6. (vi) VERTEX COVER is NP-complete, hence NP-hard.
  7. The NP-hard problems are (i), (ii), (iv) and (vi), four in all.

Answer: 4.

Common misconception. Excluding the halting problem because it is undecidable, or including 2-SAT because it looks like SAT. Hardness is a lower bound and reaches beyond NP, while polynomial-time problems are below it.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: The class co-NP is best described as:
options: the set of languages whose complements lie in NP.
the set of languages that do not belong to NP.
the set of languages decided by a nondeterministic machine that never uses its choices.
the set of languages L for which both L and its complement lie in P.

solution.concept: co-NP is defined by complementing membership, not by negating the class: L ∈ co-NP ⇔ L̄ ∈ NP.
steps: Take a language L. It lies in co-NP when a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine accepts exactly the strings outside L.
Equivalently, the complement L̄ is accepted by a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine, that is L̄ ∈ NP.
So co-NP = { L : L̄ ∈ NP }, which is option A.

Option B describes the set complement of NP as a collection of languages, which is not a complexity class defined this way; option C describes P; option D describes P as well, since P is closed under complement.
solution.final: the set of languages whose complements lie in NP — option A.
solution.trap: Reading co-NP as 'languages not in NP'. Complementation is applied inside each language, not to the class as a whole.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following inclusions is a proved theorem?
options: NP ⊆ co-NP
P ⊆ NP ∩ co-NP
NP = co-NP
co-NP ⊆ P

solution.concept: Two facts combine: a deterministic polynomial-time machine is a nondeterministic one, and P is closed under complement.
steps: Every language of P is decided by a deterministic polynomial-time machine, which is also a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine, so P ⊆ NP.
If L ∈ P then L̄ is decided by the same machine with its answer reversed, so L̄ ∈ P ⊆ NP, which gives L ∈ co-NP. Hence P ⊆ co-NP.
Combining the two inclusions gives P ⊆ NP ∩ co-NP.
NP ⊆ co-NP, NP = co-NP and co-NP ⊆ P are all open.
solution.trap: Treating NP = co-NP as known because both classes contain P. Only the weak inclusion P ⊆ NP ∩ co-NP has been proved.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: If some NP-complete language L belongs to co-NP, which of the following follows?
options: P = NP
NP = co-NP
NP ⊂ co-NP, a proper containment
L ∈ P

solution.concept: co-NP is closed under polynomial-time many-one reductions, so putting an NP-complete language inside co-NP drags all of NP along with it.
steps: Let A ∈ NP. Because L is NP-complete, A ≤p L.
co-NP is closed under polynomial-time many-one reductions: if X ≤p Y and Y ∈ co-NP then X ∈ co-NP. Hence A ∈ co-NP, so NP ⊆ co-NP.
For the other direction let B ∈ co-NP, so B̄ ∈ NP. Since L is NP-complete, B̄ ≤p L, and L ∈ co-NP gives B̄ ∈ co-NP, that is B ∈ NP. Hence co-NP ⊆ NP.
The two inclusions give NP = co-NP; nothing here forces P = NP or puts L in P.
solution.trap: Concluding P = NP. Collapsing NP with co-NP is a different question from collapsing NP with P, and neither implication is known.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: NP ⊆ PSPACE
co-NP ⊆ PSPACE
If NP = co-NP then P = NP.
P ⊆ NP ∩ co-NP

solution.concept: Polynomial space is powerful enough to simulate nondeterministic polynomial time by exhaustive search, and PSPACE is closed under complement.
steps: A: a nondeterministic machine that runs in polynomial time can be simulated by walking all computation paths depth-first; each path needs polynomial space and the space is reused, so NP ⊆ PSPACE. TRUE.
B: PSPACE is closed under complement (reverse the final answer of a deterministic polynomial-space machine), and NP ⊆ PSPACE, so co-NP ⊆ PSPACE. TRUE.
C: this is not a theorem. Collapsing NP with co-NP says nothing about deterministic time, and P = NP would remain open. FALSE.
D: P is contained in NP, and P is closed under complement, so P is contained in co-NP as well. TRUE.
solution.final: Options (A), (B) and (D) are TRUE; (C) is FALSE.
solution.trap: Assuming every collapse of two nondeterministic classes implies P = NP. NP = co-NP and P = NP are independent questions as far as anyone knows.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: How many of the following languages are known to lie in NP? (i) SAT  (ii) 3-SAT  (iii) the halting problem  (iv) the decision version of VERTEX COVER  (v) the complement of SAT

solution.concept: Membership in NP needs a polynomial-length certificate that a deterministic verifier can check in polynomial time.
steps: (i) SAT: a satisfying assignment is a certificate of linear length and can be checked in linear time. In NP.
(ii) 3-SAT: same certificate, restricted to a 3-CNF formula. In NP.
(iii) The halting problem is not even decidable, so it cannot be in NP. Not counted.
(iv) VERTEX COVER: a set of at most k vertices is a certificate, and checking that it covers every edge is linear. In NP.
(v) The complement of SAT: whether it lies in NP is exactly the open question NP = co-NP, so it is not known to be in NP. Not counted.
That leaves three languages: (i), (ii) and (iv).
solution.trap: Counting the complement of SAT, or forgetting that the halting problem is undecidable rather than merely hard. 'Not known to be in NP' is not the same as 'in NP'.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following operations preserve membership in NP? (Select all that apply.)
options: union
intersection
complement
Kleene star

solution.concept: NP is closed under the operations built from running two nondeterministic machines, but complement is the one operation that is open.
steps: Union: guess which of the two machines to run, then run it; accept if it accepts. Polynomial. CLOSED.
Intersection: run the two nondeterministic machines one after the other and accept only if both accept. Polynomial. CLOSED.
Complement: negating an NP machine would require certifying that no accepting path exists, which is not a polynomial-length witness. OPEN, so not preserved.
Kleene star: guess a split of the input into pieces and run the machine on each piece; the certificate records the split and the accepting paths. Polynomial. CLOSED.
solution.final: Union, intersection and Kleene star are closed; complement is not known to be.
solution.trap: Assuming every boolean operation is cheap. Union and intersection are constructive because they combine accepting paths; complement would have to certify the absence of a path.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following, if proved, would establish P ≠ NP?
options: An NP-complete problem for which no polynomial-time algorithm is currently known.
A language in NP that requires Ω(2ⁿ) time on infinitely many input lengths.
NP = co-NP.
An NP-hard problem that lies in P.

solution.concept: P ≠ NP is a statement about lower bounds: some language in NP must be proved to need superpolynomial time.
steps: Option A records the state of the art, not a theorem; not knowing an algorithm is not a proof that none exists.
Option B is a genuine lower bound for a language in NP, and 2ⁿ grows faster than every polynomial, so it separates NP from P.
Option C, if anything, is a collapse of two nondeterministic classes and implies nothing about deterministic time.
Option D would give P = NP: every language in NP reduces to the NP-hard language, so it would inherit a polynomial algorithm. It is the opposite of what is wanted.
solution.final: a language in NP needing Ω(2ⁿ) time — option B.
solution.trap: Treating 'no polynomial algorithm is known' as a lower bound, or picking option D which actually forces P = NP.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: A polynomial-time many-one reduction from A to B is a function f such that:
options: f is computable in polynomial time and x ∈ A ⇔ f(x) ∈ B.
f is computable in polynomial time and x ∈ A ⇒ f(x) ∈ B.
f is computable in polynomial time and x ∈ B ⇔ f(x) ∈ A.
f is a polynomial-time bijection from A onto B.

solution.concept: A reduction must translate membership exactly, in both directions, and be fast enough to compose with a polynomial-time solver.
steps: The forward direction x ∈ A ⇒ f(x) ∈ B alone is satisfied by the constant map into B and carries no information.
The biconditional x ∈ A ⇔ f(x) ∈ B makes deciding B decide A, which is the point of a reduction.
Polynomial-time computability keeps the composition polynomial.
Option C reverses the arrow (it reduces B to A); option D demands far more than a reduction needs, and no bijection is required.
solution.final: polynomial-time computable with x ∈ A ⇔ f(x) ∈ B — option A.
solution.trap: Accepting the one-way implication. Hardness proofs and easiness proofs both depend on the 'no' instances being preserved as well.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: If A ≤p B and B ∈ P, which of the following follows?
options: A ∈ P
B ≤p A
A is NP-complete
nothing can be concluded about A

solution.concept: Easiness transfers backwards along a reduction: an easy target makes the source easy.
steps: On input x, first compute f(x) in polynomial time; the reduction guarantees x ∈ A ⇔ f(x) ∈ B.
Then run the polynomial-time decider for B on f(x) and return its answer.
Both stages are polynomial, and their composition is polynomial, so A is decided in polynomial time.
Nothing follows about B ≤p A, and A need not be NP-complete; in fact A ∈ P rules that out unless P = NP.
solution.trap: Reversing the arrow and concluding something about B, or assuming every language that reduces to an easy problem is itself NP-complete.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: A reduction from A to B runs in O(n²) time and, on an instance of length n, produces an instance of length O(n³). The decider for B runs in O(m²) on an instance of length m. The composed algorithm decides A in O(n^k). Give the smallest integer k.

solution.concept: Compose the two costs: the solver's cost must be measured on the length of the instance the reduction produced.
steps: The reduction costs O(n²).
The instance handed to the solver has length m = O(n³).
Substituting into the solver's bound gives O(m²) = O((n³)²) = O(n⁶).
The total is O(n² + n⁶) = O(n⁶), since the degree-6 term dominates.
So the smallest such integer is 6.
solution.trap: Multiplying the exponents (2 × 3 = 6 is a coincidence here) or adding the two bounds as n² · n². The substitution is of the produced length into the solver's polynomial, which raises the exponent to 3 × 2.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following statements about polynomial-time many-one reductions are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: If A ≤p B and B ∈ NP then A ∈ NP.
If A ≤p B and B ≤p C then A ≤p C.
If A ≤p B then B ≤p A.
If A ≤p B and B ∈ P then A ∈ P.

solution.concept: Membership in NP and in P both travel backwards along a reduction, and reductions compose; reducibility itself is a preorder, not a symmetric relation.
steps: A: given a verifier for B, verify f(x) with the same certificate, so A has a polynomial-time verifier. TRUE.
B: compute g(f(x)); a composition of two polynomial-time functions is polynomial, and the biconditional chains. TRUE.
C: ≤p is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric. An easy language reduces to a hard one, and the reverse map need not exist. FALSE.
D: compose the reduction with the polynomial decider for B. TRUE.
solution.final: Options (A), (B) and (D) are TRUE; (C) is FALSE.
solution.trap: Treating ≤p as if it were an equivalence. Two mutually reducible problems are equally hard, but one-directional reducibility only orders them.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: To prove that a new decision problem X is NP-complete it is enough to show:
options: X ∈ NP and X ≤p 3-SAT.
X ∈ NP and 3-SAT ≤p X.
X is NP-hard and X ≤p SAT.
X ∈ NP and every problem in NP reduces to X in exponential time.

solution.concept: NP-completeness = membership in NP + hardness, and hardness is proved by reducing a known NP-complete problem to the new one.
steps: X ∈ NP supplies the upper bound.
3-SAT ≤p X, together with 3-SAT being NP-hard, gives that every language of NP reduces to X by transitivity. That is the lower bound.
Option A reduces X to an easy-to-state but already hard problem, which only shows X is no harder than 3-SAT.
Option C omits membership in NP, and exponential-time reductions are too weak to preserve polynomial solvability.
Option D is not a polynomial-time reduction at all, so it proves nothing about P versus NP.
solution.final: X ∈ NP and 3-SAT ≤p X — option B.
solution.trap: Reducing the new problem to a known NP-complete one. That direction shows X ∈ NP at best; the known hard problem must reduce to X.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: If A ≤p B and B ∈ P then A ∈ P.
If A ≤p B and B is NP-hard then A is NP-hard.
If A ≤p B and B ∈ NP then A ∈ NP.
If A is NP-complete, A ≤p B and B ∈ NP, then B is NP-complete.

solution.concept: Everything follows from the direction of the arrow: easiness and membership flow backwards, hardness flows forwards.
steps: A is true: compute f(x) and run the polynomial-time decider for B on it; the composition is polynomial.
C is true: run B's polynomial-time verifier on f(x) with the same certificate; the composition is still a polynomial-time verifier for A.
D is true: B ∈ NP gives the upper bound, and every language of NP reduces to A, which reduces to B, so B is NP-hard as well.
B is false. A ≤p B makes A no harder than B, so a hard target says nothing about the source: A could be 2-SAT while B is SAT.
Hence exactly one statement fails, and it is the one that pushes hardness backwards along the arrow.
solution.trap: Reading A ≤p B as "A is at least as hard as B". The arrow points from the easier problem to the harder one, so hardness is inherited by the target, never by the source.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following decision problems is known to lie in P?
options: CLIQUE
2-SAT
3-SAT
VERTEX COVER

solution.concept: Restricting clauses to at most two literals removes the hardness: 2-SAT is decided in linear time through the implication graph.
steps: Build the implication graph with an edge (a → b) for every clause (¬a ∨ b) and an edge (b → a) for the same clause read the other way.
The formula is unsatisfiable exactly when some variable and its negation lie in the same strongly connected component.
Strongly connected components are found in linear time, so 2-SAT is in P.
CLIQUE, 3-SAT and VERTEX COVER are all NP-complete, so no polynomial algorithm is known for them.
solution.trap: Assuming that a problem that shares the name SAT must be hard. The two-literal restriction is what makes 2-SAT tractable.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: The decision version of VERTEX COVER asks, given a graph G and an integer k, whether:
options: G has a vertex cover of size at most k.
G has a vertex cover of size exactly k.
every edge of G belongs to some vertex cover of size k.
G has a minimum vertex cover that is unique.

solution.concept: The decision version of a minimisation problem asks a yes/no question with a threshold, not for the optimum value.
steps: A vertex cover is a set S of vertices such that every edge has at least one endpoint in S.
The decision problem fixes a bound k and asks whether some cover of size at most k exists.
'At most' is essential: a cover of size less than k can always be padded, so 'exactly k' is a different and less natural question.
Uniqueness of the minimum cover is a separate structural question and is not part of the standard decision problem.
solution.final: whether G has a vertex cover of size at most k — option A.
solution.trap: Confusing the decision version with the optimisation version, which asks for the minimum size. Only decision problems have a membership in NP.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: In the standard reduction from 3-SAT to CLIQUE, a 3-CNF formula with 5 clauses and 3 literals per clause is turned into a graph. Give the value of k, the target clique size, used in the reduction.

solution.concept: The reduction creates one vertex per literal occurrence and joins two vertices unless they are in the same clause or are complementary literals.
steps: One vertex is created for each literal occurrence, so the graph has 5 × 3 = 15 vertices.
Vertices inside the same clause are never adjacent, so a clique contains at most one vertex per clause.
A clique of size equal to the number of clauses picks exactly one literal from each clause, and the construction forbids complementary pairs.
So the target size is the number of clauses, k = 5.
solution.trap: Answering 15 (the number of vertices) or 3 (the literals per clause). The target is the number of clauses.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: A 3-CNF formula has 4 clauses, each with exactly 3 literals. The standard reduction builds a graph on 12 vertices and a target clique of size 4. If VERTEX COVER is then asked on the complement of that graph, what is the smallest k for which the formula is satisfiable exactly when the graph has a vertex cover of size at most k?

solution.concept: In the complement graph a clique becomes an independent set, and the complement of an independent set is a vertex cover.
steps: The 3-SAT to CLIQUE construction gives a graph H on 12 vertices in which the formula is satisfiable exactly when H has a clique of size 4.
Take the complement graph H̄. A clique of size 4 in H is an independent set of size 4 in H̄.
In any graph, the complement of an independent set is a vertex cover, so an independent set of size 4 leaves a vertex cover of size 12 − 4 = 8.
Sizes add up to the number of vertices, so the smallest such k is 8.
solution.trap: Answering 4 by keeping the same size, or 16 by adding instead of subtracting. The correspondence is a complement of the vertex set, so the two sizes sum to n.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following problems are NP-complete? (Select all that apply.)
options: 3-SAT
VERTEX COVER (decision version)
deciding whether a graph is bipartite
HAMILTONIAN CYCLE

solution.concept: The NP-complete members of this list are the ones that stay hard on general graphs; the tractable one has a linear-time characterisation.
steps: 3-SAT is NP-complete: SAT reduces to it by splitting long clauses, and it is in NP through a truth-assignment certificate.
VERTEX COVER is NP-complete, by a reduction from CLIQUE through the complement graph.
Bipartiteness is in P: a BFS 2-colouring either succeeds or exposes an odd cycle, in linear time. So it is not NP-complete unless P = NP.
HAMILTONIAN CYCLE is NP-complete, by a reduction from VERTEX COVER or from 3-SAT.
solution.final: 3-SAT, VERTEX COVER and HAMILTONIAN CYCLE; bipartiteness is in P.
solution.trap: Including bipartiteness because it mentions graphs, or excluding HAMILTONIAN CYCLE because the Eulerian analogue is easy. Eulerian is a degree condition; Hamiltonian is not.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: The standard reduction from CLIQUE to INDEPENDENT SET works by:
options: taking the complement graph and keeping the same k.
keeping the graph unchanged and setting k′ = n − k.
taking the complement graph and setting k′ = n − k.
deleting one vertex from the graph and keeping k.

solution.concept: A clique in G is exactly an independent set in the complement graph, with the same vertex set and the same size.
steps: Two vertices are adjacent in the complement exactly when they are non-adjacent in G.
A set S is a clique in G when every pair of its vertices is adjacent in G, that is, no pair is adjacent in the complement.
That is exactly the condition for S to be independent in the complement graph.
So the same S and the same k witness both problems, and the reduction keeps k unchanged.
solution.final: complement graph with the same k — option A.
solution.trap: Changing k as well. Mixing the two operations gives a reduction to VERTEX COVER, not to INDEPENDENT SET.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: In the reduction from 3-SAT to CLIQUE, which of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The formula is satisfiable iff the graph has a clique of size equal to the number of clauses, and such a clique picks one literal per clause without picking a literal together with its negation.
The graph has a clique of size equal to the number of clauses iff the formula is unsatisfiable.
A clique of maximum size may contain two vertices that come from the same clause.
The reduction runs in polynomial time only when the formula is satisfiable.

solution.concept: The reduction encodes each literal occurrence as a vertex and forbids exactly the two ways a set of literals can fail to be a partial assignment.
steps: Vertices of the same clause are left non-adjacent, so a clique holds at most one literal per clause; reaching the number of clauses therefore means exactly one per clause.
Complementary literals are left non-adjacent, so a clique never contains both x and ¬x.
Such a clique is a consistent partial assignment that satisfies one literal in every clause, which extends to a full satisfying assignment.
Conversely a satisfying assignment supplies one true literal per clause, and those vertices are pairwise adjacent.
The construction is a fixed polynomial-time procedure and is carried out whatever the formula is, so option D is false, and options B and C contradict the two non-adjacency rules.
solution.trap: Believing the reduction needs the formula to be satisfiable, or that the graph can encode two literals of one clause. Both non-adjacency rules are what make the correspondence exact in both directions.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: A language L is NP-hard exactly when:
options: every language in NP reduces to L in polynomial time.
L reduces to every language in NP in polynomial time.
L ∈ NP and every language in NP reduces to L.
L is not in P.

solution.concept: NP-hardness is a lower bound: L is at least as hard as everything in NP.
steps: The definition quantifies over the languages of NP: for every A ∈ NP, A ≤p L.
Membership of L in NP is not required; adding it gives NP-completeness, which is option C.
Option B reverses the arrow and describes a language that is no harder than NP.
Option D is neither necessary nor sufficient: undecidable languages are NP-hard yet not in P, and the question P versus NP is open.
solution.final: every language in NP reduces to L — option A.
solution.trap: Building NP membership into the definition, which turns NP-hard into NP-complete and wrongly excludes the halting problem and optimisation problems.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following is NP-hard but not known to belong to NP?
options: SAT
VERTEX COVER (decision version)
finding the chromatic number of a graph
2-SAT

solution.concept: NP contains decision problems only. A minimisation problem can be NP-hard and still lie outside NP, because it has no yes/no answer to certify.
steps: SAT and VERTEX COVER are decision problems in NP, and both are NP-complete, so they are not the answer.
2-SAT is in P and therefore not NP-hard unless P = NP.
The chromatic number is a number to be computed, so 'find the chromatic number' is not a language with a yes/no answer and is not a member of NP.
It is NP-hard, because the decision problem 'is the chromatic number at most 3?' is NP-complete and an algorithm for the number settles it.
Hence it is NP-hard without being known to lie in NP.
solution.final: finding the chromatic number — option C.
solution.trap: Assuming every NP-hard problem must be in NP. Optimisation problems are the standard counterexamples; the halting problem is the extreme one.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every NP-complete language is NP-hard.
Every NP-hard language belongs to NP.
If P = NP then every NP-hard language lies in P.
If an NP-hard language lies in P then P = NP.

solution.concept: NP-hard is a lower bound that reaches beyond NP, so it is inherited by NP-complete languages and it collapses P and NP when it meets P.
steps: A: NP-completeness is defined as NP-hard together with membership in NP, so the hardness half holds by definition. TRUE.
B: the halting problem is NP-hard, since SAT reduces to it, yet it is undecidable and so not in NP. FALSE.
C: even with P = NP, an NP-hard language may be undecidable, so it need not lie in P. FALSE.
D: if L ∈ P is NP-hard then every A ∈ NP satisfies A ≤p L, and easiness transfers backwards, so A ∈ P and NP ⊆ P. TRUE.
solution.final: Options (A) and (D) are TRUE; (B) and (C) are FALSE.
solution.trap: Option C looks harmless but forgets that NP-hardness is not confined to decidable problems. A collapse of P and NP does not make the halting problem decidable.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: How many of the following languages are NP-hard? (i) SAT  (ii) the halting problem  (iii) 2-SAT  (iv) the decision version of VERTEX COVER  (v) the set of primes written in binary

solution.concept: Hardness needs every language of NP to reduce to the problem; problems in P qualify only if P = NP, and undecidable problems can qualify.
steps: (i) SAT is NP-complete, hence NP-hard.
(ii) The halting problem is NP-hard: SAT reduces to it, since a decider for halting would decide satisfiability by simulating a search.
(iii) 2-SAT is in P, so it is NP-hard only if P = NP; it is not known to be.
(iv) VERTEX COVER is NP-complete, hence NP-hard.
(v) Primality is in P (the AKS algorithm), so it is not known to be NP-hard.
The NP-hard members are (i), (ii) and (iv), three in all.
solution.trap: Excluding the halting problem because it is undecidable, or including 2-SAT and primality because they are about hard-looking search. Membership in P rules hardness out unless P = NP.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: If P ≠ NP, which of the following must hold?
options: No NP-complete language lies in P.
NP = co-NP
Every NP-hard language is undecidable.
2-SAT is NP-complete.

solution.concept: An NP-complete language in P would drag all of NP into P, so P ≠ NP forbids it.
steps: Suppose an NP-complete L lay in P. Every A ∈ NP reduces to L, and easiness transfers backwards, so A ∈ P and P = NP.
Since we assume P ≠ NP, no NP-complete language lies in P.
NP = co-NP is an independent open question and is not implied either way.
NP-hard languages include decidable ones such as SAT, so they are not all undecidable.
2-SAT is in P, so it cannot be NP-complete when P ≠ NP.
solution.final: no NP-complete language lies in P — option A.
solution.trap: Believing P ≠ NP also settles NP versus co-NP, or that hardness forces undecidability. The two questions are separate.

questions.question: For the two functions f(n) = 2ⁿ⁺¹ and g(n) = 2ⁿ, which of the following is TRUE?
options: f(n) = Θ(g(n))
f(n) = O(g(n)) but f(n) ≠ Θ(g(n))
f(n) = ω(g(n))
f(n) = o(g(n))

solution.concept: A constant factor is invisible to Θ. Here 2ⁿ⁺¹ = 2 · 2ⁿ exactly, so the two functions differ by the constant 2 at every n.
steps: Write the ratio: f(n)/g(n) = 2ⁿ⁺¹ / 2ⁿ = 2 for every n.
A constant ratio c means f = Θ(g) with both constants equal to 2.
Since the ratio is neither 0 nor ∞, the functions are of the same order.
solution.trap: Reading the +1 in the exponent as an extra factor of n. An additive change in the exponent is a constant multiplier, which Θ ignores; only a multiplicative change in n would separate the classes.

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE?
options: log₂(n!) = Θ(n log₂ n)
log₂(n!) = Θ(n)
log₂(n!) = Θ(n²)
log₂(n!) = O(log₂ n)

solution.concept: log(n!) is a sum of n logarithmic terms, and a sum is trapped between its smallest and largest term times the number of terms.
steps: Write log₂(n!) = Σk=1..n log₂ k.
Upper bound: every term is at most log₂ n, so the sum is at most n log₂ n.
Lower bound: the last ⌈n/2⌉ terms are each at least log₂(n/2) = log₂ n − 1, so the sum is at least (n/2)(log₂ n − 1).
Both bounds are Θ(n log n), so log₂(n!) = Θ(n log₂ n). This is the weak form of Stirling's approximation.
solution.trap: Answering Θ(n) because "log of a factorial feels linear". The factorial has n factors and each contributes a logarithm, so the product of that many log-sized terms is n log n.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: log₂ n = O(n⁰·¹)
n⁰·¹ = O(log₂ n)
n log₂ n = O(n¹·¹)
2^(log₂ n) = Θ(n)

solution.concept: Every positive power of n eventually outgrows every power of log n, however small the exponent on n and however large the power on the log.
steps: Option B asks whether n⁰·¹ / log₂ n is bounded. It tends to ∞, so the statement is false.
Option A is the same ratio inverted, and it tends to 0, so it is true.
Option C: n log n / n¹·¹ = log n / n⁰·¹ → 0, so it is true.
Option D: 2^(log₂ n) = n identically, so it is true.
solution.trap: Options A and B look symmetric and both get marked true. The asymmetry is real: the logarithm is the slower-growing side, so log n is dominated by any positive power of n.

questions.question: Let f(n) = n^(log₂ n) / 2ⁿ. Which of the following is TRUE?
options: f(n) = ω(1)
f(n) = Θ(1)
f(n) = o(1)
f(n) = Ω(n)

solution.concept: Convert everything to one base. n^(log₂ n) = 2^((log₂ n)²), so the whole function is a single power of 2 with a comparison of exponents inside it.
steps: Rewrite the numerator: n^(log₂ n) = (2^(log₂ n))^(log₂ n) = 2^((log₂ n)²).
So f(n) = 2^((log₂ n)² − n).
The exponent (log₂ n)² − n tends to −∞, because a squared logarithm grows slower than n.
Hence f(n) → 0, which is the definition of f(n) = o(1).
solution.trap: The numerator grows faster than any fixed power of n, which tempts an answer of ω(1). But 2ⁿ is a full exponential, and an exponential beats any n^(log n).

questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: 3ⁿ = O(2ⁿ)
√n = O(n^(2/3))
n² / log₂ n = ω(n)
log₂(n²) = Θ(log₂ n)

solution.concept: Compare two functions by the limit of their ratio: a limit of 0 means little-o, a finite non-zero limit means Θ, and a limit of ∞ means ω.
steps: A: 3ⁿ / 2ⁿ = (3/2)ⁿ → ∞, so 3ⁿ is not O(2ⁿ). This statement is false.
B: n^(1/2) / n^(2/3) = n^(−1/6) → 0, so √n is strictly smaller, and the statement holds.
C: (n²/log n) / n = n / log n → ∞, so the statement holds.
D: log₂(n²) = 2 log₂ n, a constant multiple, so the statement holds.
solution.trap: Option A is the usual slip: for exponentials the larger base always wins, so 3ⁿ overtakes 2ⁿ and no constant rescues it. Option C is misjudged by assuming that dividing by log n turns n² into n.

questions.question: For f(n) = 100n + 5000 and g(n) = n², the smallest integer n₀ such that f(n) ≤ g(n) for every n ≥ n₀ is ____.

solution.concept: The witness n₀ of a big-O statement comes from solving the defining inequality, not from estimating it.
steps: Solve n² ≥ 100n + 5000, that is n² − 100n − 5000 ≥ 0.
The roots are (100 ± √(10000 + 20000)) / 2 = (100 ± 173·2) / 2, giving about 136·6 and −36·6.
So the inequality holds for n ≥ 136·6, and the smallest integer candidate is 137.
Check the boundary: at n = 136, f = 18600 and g = 18496, so it fails; at n = 137, f = 18700 and g = 18769, so it holds.
solution.trap: Rounding 136·6 down to 136 because "n₀ can be any large number". The smallest valid integer must be checked at the boundary, and 136 fails.

questions.question: For asymptotically positive functions f and g, f(n) = o(g(n)) holds exactly when which of the following are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: For every constant c > 0 there is n₀ with f(n) < c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.
There is a constant c > 0 with f(n) < c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.
f(n) / g(n) → ∞ as n → ∞.
f(n) = O(g(n)) and f(n) ≠ Θ(g(n)).

solution.concept: Little-o is big-O with the quantifier strengthened from "some constant" to "every constant". The two definitions differ only in that word.
steps: The definition of o(g) quantifies over all constants c > 0, which is option A.
Option B is exactly the definition of O(g), so it characterises big-O, not little-o.
Option C describes ω(g), the opposite relation.
For positive functions o(g) = O(g) − Θ(g): a function is little-o exactly when it is big-O but not of the same order. That is option D.
solution.trap: Choosing B, because "a constant works" is what most students remember. The single word "every" is what separates o from O.

questions.question: Using the Master Theorem, the solution of T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n is:
options: Θ(n²)
Θ(n log n)
Θ(n² log n)
Θ(n)

solution.concept: Case 1 of the Master Theorem: when the driving function is polynomially smaller than the watershed n^(log_b a), the recursion (the leaves) dominates.
steps: Here a = 4 and b = 2, so the watershed is n^(log₂ 4) = n².
The driving function is f(n) = n, and n = O(n^(2−ε)) with ε = 1, a polynomial gap.
Case 1 therefore applies and T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)) = Θ(n²).
solution.trap: Reading f(n) = n and answering Θ(n). In case 1 the root contributes only n; the n² leaves are what the Θ-class records.

questions.question: The solution of T(n) = 16T(n/4) + n² is:
options: Θ(n²)
Θ(n log n)
Θ(n³)
Θ(n² log n)

solution.concept: Case 2: when the driving function matches the watershed exactly, every level costs the same and an extra logarithmic factor appears.
steps: a = 16 and b = 4, so the watershed is n^(log₄ 16) = n².
The driving function is f(n) = n², exactly the watershed, so case 2 applies.
Case 2 gives T(n) = Θ(n² log n).
A sanity check from the recursion tree: level i holds 16ⁱ nodes of size n/4ⁱ, and 16ⁱ·(n/4ⁱ)² = n² at every level, over log₄ n + 1 levels.
solution.trap: Dropping the extra log factor and answering Θ(n²). Balance between the two sides is precisely the case where the level cost never decays, so the log cannot be dropped.

questions.question: Consider T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n / log₂ n. Which of the following statements is TRUE?
options: Case 1 applies, so T(n) = Θ(n).
Case 2 applies, so T(n) = Θ(n log n).
None of the three cases applies, although T(n) = Θ(n log log n).
Case 3 applies, so T(n) = Θ(n log n).

solution.concept: The three cases need a polynomial gap: f must be smaller or larger than the watershed by a factor n^ε. A factor of only log n leaves a gap the theorem cannot classify.
steps: The watershed is n^(log₂ 2) = n.
Here f(n)/n = 1/log₂ n → 0, so f is smaller than the watershed.
But f is not polynomially smaller: for every ε > 0, n^ε / log₂ n → ∞, so no ε satisfies the case-1 requirement.
So none of the three cases applies. The recurrence is still solvable by other means, and the known solution is Θ(n log log n).
solution.trap: "f grows slower than the watershed, therefore case 1" is the trap. Case 1 demands a polynomial gap; a logarithmic gap falls between the cases.

questions.question: The solution of T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n√n is:
options: Θ(n)
Θ(n log n)
Θ(n^(3/2))
Θ(n²)

solution.concept: Case 3: the driving function is polynomially larger than the watershed, provided the regularity condition a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n) holds for some c < 1.
steps: The watershed is n^(log₂ 2) = n, and f(n) = n^(3/2) is polynomially larger with ε = 1/2.
Check regularity: 2·(n/2)^(3/2) = 2·n^(3/2)/(2√2) = n^(3/2)/√2.
So a·f(n/b) = (1/√2)·f(n) with c = 1/√2 < 1, and the condition holds.
Case 3 gives T(n) = Θ(f(n)) = Θ(n^(3/2)).
solution.trap: Applying case 3 without checking regularity. The condition is not decoration: it is what guarantees the root cost dominates the sum, and here it holds with c = 1/√2.

questions.question: For which of the following recurrences does case 3 of the Master Theorem apply, with its regularity condition satisfied? (Select all that apply.)
options: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n²
T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n³
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n²

solution.concept: Case 3 needs two things at once: f polynomially larger than n^(log_b a), and a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n) for some constant c < 1.
steps: A: watershed n^(log₂ 2) = n, f = n² is larger, and 2·(n/2)² = 0·5n² ≤ 0·5·f(n), so case 3 applies.
B: watershed n^(log₂ 4) = n², f = n³ is larger, and 4·(n/2)³ = 0·5n³ ≤ 0·5·f(n), so case 3 applies.
C: watershed n and f = n are equal, so this is case 2, giving Θ(n log n).
D: watershed n^(log₂ 8) = n³ and f = n² is smaller, so this is case 1, giving Θ(n³).
solution.trap: Option C is forced into case 3 because f(n) = n "matches the n in the watershed". Equality of orders is case 2, not case 3.

questions.question: For T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n² log₂ n, the extended Master Theorem gives T(n) = Θ(n² log^k n). The value of k is ____.

solution.concept: Extended case 2: if f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log^k n) for k ≥ 0, the solution is Θ(n^(log_b a) · log^(k+1) n). The log exponent increases by one.
steps: a = 4 and b = 2, so the watershed is n^(log₂ 4) = n².
Write f in watershed form: n² log₂ n = Θ(n² · log¹ n), so k = 1.
The extended case adds one to the exponent of the log, giving T(n) = Θ(n² log² n).
Matching Θ(n² log^k n) gives k = 2.
solution.trap: Reporting k = 1, the exponent read straight off f(n). The extended case always adds one more log factor, so the answer is k + 1.

questions.question: The solution of T(n) = 2T(n/2) + √n is:
options: Θ(√n)
Θ(n)
Θ(√n log n)
Θ(n log n)

solution.concept: In a recursion tree, add the per-level costs. Here the level cost grows geometrically, so the deepest level dominates the sum.
steps: At depth i there are 2ⁱ nodes, each of size n/2ⁱ, so the level cost is 2ⁱ·√(n/2ⁱ) = √n · 2^(i/2).
The level cost increases with i by a factor √2, so the levels form a geometric series with ratio √2 > 1.
The tree has depth log₂ n, so the last level costs √n · 2^(log₂ n / 2) = √n · √n = n.
A geometric series is dominated by its largest term, so the total is Θ(n).
solution.trap: Answering Θ(√n log n) by assuming every level costs √n as it does for T(n) = 2T(n/4) + √n. Here the divisor is 2, not 4, so the level cost grows instead of staying flat.

questions.question: In the recursion tree for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n², the total cost of all nodes at depth i (the root is at depth 0) is:
options: n² / 2ⁱ
n²
2ⁱ · n²
n² / 4ⁱ

solution.concept: Level cost = (number of nodes at that depth) × (cost of one node at that depth).
steps: The recursion doubles, so depth i has 2ⁱ nodes.
Each node at depth i represents a subproblem of size n/2ⁱ, and its own cost is that size squared, n²/4ⁱ.
Multiply: 2ⁱ · n²/4ⁱ = n²/2ⁱ.
The level costs halve at each step, so the root dominates and the total is Θ(n²).
solution.trap: Option D forgets the 2ⁱ nodes and reports only the per-node cost; option B forgets to square the shrinking size. Both look plausible, and only the product is right.

questions.question: For T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n with T(1) = 1 and n = 2^k, the total cost contributed by the leaves of the recursion tree is:
options: n
n log n
n²
4n

solution.concept: Leaves of a recursion tree cost (number of leaves) × (cost of the base case).
steps: Each node has 4 children, so depth i holds 4ⁱ nodes.
The tree reaches size 1 after k = log₂ n levels, so the number of leaves is 4^k = 4^(log₂ n).
Rewrite in base n: 4^(log₂ n) = n^(log₂ 4) = n².
Each leaf costs T(1) = 1, so the leaves contribute n² in total, which is also the Θ-class of the whole recurrence.
solution.trap: Multiplying the leaf count n² by the subproblem size at the leaves (which is 1, not n). Counting leaves is enough here; their per-node cost is the constant 1.

questions.question: In the recursion tree for T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n², the total cost of all nodes at depth i is:
options: n² / 3ⁱ
n² / 9ⁱ
3ⁱ · n²
n²

solution.concept: A level cost stays constant exactly when the branching factor equals the square of the shrinking factor, that is when a = b² here.
steps: Depth i has 9ⁱ nodes, each of size n/3ⁱ.
A node of size n/3ⁱ costs (n/3ⁱ)² = n²/9ⁱ.
Multiply: 9ⁱ · n²/9ⁱ = n², the same at every depth.
With log₃ n + 1 levels each costing n², the total is Θ(n² log n).
solution.trap: Expecting the decay seen in T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n². There the level cost halves; here 9·(1/3)² = 1, so nothing decays and the extra log factor appears.

questions.question: For T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n with T(1) = 1, which of the following statements about its recursion tree are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The number of leaves is n^(log₂ 3).
The total cost of the nodes at depth i is (3/2)ⁱ · n.
T(n) = Θ(n^(log₂ 3)).
T(n) = Θ(n log n).

solution.concept: When each level costs a constant factor more than the level above it, the leaves dominate the sum.
steps: Depth i has 3ⁱ nodes of size n/2ⁱ, so its cost is 3ⁱ · (n/2ⁱ) = (3/2)ⁱ · n, confirming option B.
The tree has log₂ n levels, so the number of leaves is 3^(log₂ n) = n^(log₂ 3), confirming option A.
The level costs form a geometric series with ratio 3/2 > 1, so the total is dominated by the last level: Θ((3/2)^(log₂ n) · n) = Θ(n^(log₂ 3)). Option C holds.
Since log₂ 3 ≈ 1·585, the solution grows faster than n log n, so option D is false.
solution.trap: Option D: the tree is unbalanced in cost but balanced in depth, and students read balanced depth as "n log n". Because the level cost grows, the leaves, not the top levels, set the total.

questions.question: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n² with T(1) = 1, the total number of nodes in the recursion tree when n = 4 is ____.

solution.concept: The recursion tree stops branching when a subproblem reaches the base-case size of 1.
steps: Depth 0: one node of size 4.
Depth 1: two nodes of size 2.
Depth 2: each size-2 node splits into two size-1 nodes, giving four nodes, which are base cases.
Total: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 nodes.
solution.trap: Stopping one level early and counting 1 + 2 = 3, or counting only the four leaves. Every node in the tree, internal and leaf, is counted.

questions.question: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n² with T(1) = 1, the exact value of T(4) is:

solution.concept: An exact value is computed bottom-up from the base case; the asymptotic class says nothing about the constants.
steps: Base: T(1) = 1.
solution.trap: Substituting n = 4 into the asymptotic answer Θ(n²) and reporting 16, or doubling it to 32. The exact value carries the T(2) subtrees as well.

questions.question: The substitution method establishes an asymptotic bound on a recurrence by:
options: computing T(1), T(2), T(3) and extrapolating the pattern.
expanding the recurrence level by level into a tree and summing each level.
matching the recurrence against one of the three Master Theorem cases.
guessing a bound and proving it by induction on n.

solution.concept: The substitution method is guess-and-verify: propose a bound, then prove it by induction using the same bound on smaller inputs.
steps: Guess a candidate bound, for example T(n) ≤ c n log n.
Assume the bound for the subproblem sizes appearing on the right-hand side.
Substitute that assumption and show the bound holds for n, choosing constants as needed.
Repeat with the reversed inequality for a lower bound; together they give Θ.
solution.trap: Option A: a few computed values can suggest a guess but never prove one, and option B describes the recursion-tree method, which is a different technique.

questions.question: To prove T(n) = T(n/2) + n = O(n) by substitution, assume T(n/2) ≤ c·(n/2). The induction closes provided:
options: c ≥ 1
c ≥ 2
any constant c > 0 works
no constant works

solution.concept: After substitution, the inductive step becomes an inequality in c; the smallest constant satisfying it is the answer.
steps: Substitute: T(n) ≤ c·(n/2) + n = n·(c/2 + 1).
For the induction to close we need n·(c/2 + 1) ≤ c·n, that is c/2 + 1 ≤ c.
This reduces to c ≥ 2.
So the guess works for every c ≥ 2, and the base case is absorbed by enlarging c if necessary.
solution.trap: Choosing c ≥ 1 by matching the coefficient of n in f(n). The subproblem already contributes c/2, so the constant has to cover both the subproblem and the root.

questions.question: Consider T(n) = T(⌈n/2⌉) + T(⌊n/2⌋) + n with T(1) = 1. Which of the following are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: T(n) = Ω(n log₂ n)
T(n) = O(n log₂ n)
T(n) = Θ(n²)
T(n) = Θ(n log₂ n)

solution.concept: Floors and ceilings split n into two parts that sum to n, so they change constants but never the order. This is the merge-sort recurrence.
steps: The two subproblem sizes ⌈n/2⌉ and ⌊n/2⌋ sum to n, so every level of the recursion costs exactly n in total.
The depth is ⌈log₂ n⌉, because each step halves the size; ceilings add at most one level.
Hence T(n) ≤ n(⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1) = O(n log n) and T(n) ≥ n·log₂ n = Ω(n log n).
The two bounds meet, so T(n) = Θ(n log n): options A, B and D hold and C does not.
solution.trap: Option C: a per-level cost of n repeated log n times is n log n, not n². Multiplying the two factors as if both were n is the standard slip.

questions.question: Let T(1) = 1 and T(n) = T(n/2) + n for n > 1. The value of T(8) is ____.

solution.concept: Unroll the recurrence from the top until the base case is reached, then add the terms back up.
steps: Equivalently, T(8) = 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15.
solution.trap: Summing 8 + 4 + 2 = 14 and dropping the base case. The unrolling ends at T(1) = 1, which is part of the total.

questions.question: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n² with T(1) = 1, the smallest integer c for which the guess T(n) ≤ c·n² holds for every n ≥ 1 is ____.

solution.concept: Unrolling gives a geometric series; bounding that series gives the constant, and the base case must be checked separately.
steps: Level i of the recursion costs 2ⁱ·(n/2ⁱ)² = n²/2ⁱ.
Summing down to the base case, T(n) = n²(1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … ) < 2n², so c = 2 is enough.
Check that no smaller integer works: T(2) = 2·1 + 4 = 6, and 6 > 1·2² = 4, so c = 1 fails.
Therefore the smallest integer constant is 2.
solution.trap: Testing only n = 1, where T(1) = 1 ≤ c for any c ≥ 1, and concluding c = 1. The binding constraint appears at n = 2, where the root term n² is already paid.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: The merge step of merge sort combines two sorted runs of sizes m and n. What is the smallest number of key comparisons the merge can perform?
options: min(m, n)
max(m, n)
m + n − 1
0

solution.concept: A two-way merge walks two pointers and compares only while both runs still have keys, so the number of comparisons depends on how the two runs interleave, not on their total length.
steps: A comparison is made only while both runs are non-empty; once one run is exhausted the rest of the other run is copied without comparing.
The merge stops comparing exactly when the shorter run is exhausted, and exhausting a run of size min(m, n) takes at least one comparison per key of that run.
That lower bound is attained: when every key of the shorter run is smaller than every key of the longer one, the merge takes one key of the shorter run per comparison and then copies the rest.
So the minimum is min(m, n).
solution.trap: Reaching for m + n − 1, the maximum, out of habit. The maximum needs the runs to interleave until one key remains; the minimum needs them not to interleave at all.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: A merge step is stable only if it breaks ties in one particular way. Which convention makes the two-way merge of merge sort stable?
options: When the two current keys are equal, take the key from the left run first.
When the two current keys are equal, take the key from the right run first.
When the two current keys are equal, take the key from the longer run first.
No convention can make a merge stable, because the two runs are already interleaved.

solution.concept: Stability means equal keys keep their original relative order. In merge sort the left run always holds keys that came earlier in the input, so a tie must be resolved in favour of the left run.
steps: The left run holds the earlier positions of the input; the right run holds the later ones.
If the right key is taken on a tie, an equal key that originally stood later is written first, and the relative order of the two equal keys is reversed.
Taking the left key on a tie keeps the earlier key earlier, at every level of the recursion.
Because the merge is stable and the split is by position, merge sort is stable overall.
solution.final: Take the left run on a tie — option A.
solution.trap: Believing that stability is a property of the comparison alone. It is a property of the tie-break rule, and a single else branch decides it.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Quicksort uses the Lomuto partition with the last element of each subarray as the pivot. On the input 1, 2, …, n, already in increasing order, how many key comparisons does the whole run perform?
options: n(n − 1)/2
n log₂ n
n − 1
n²/2 + 1

solution.concept: On sorted input with the last element as pivot, every pivot is the largest key of its subarray, so each partition peels off exactly one element and the subproblem shrinks by one.
steps: On a subarray of size s the pivot is the maximum, so the loop compares it with each of the other s − 1 keys and places it at the end.
The left part therefore has s − 1 keys and the right part is empty: T(s) = T(s − 1) + (s − 1).
Unrolling gives (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2.
This is the worst case of quicksort, and sorted input reaches it whenever the pivot rule picks an extreme key.
solution.trap: Assuming the sorted input is the good case because the array is already ordered. The order of the input is irrelevant; what matters is where the pivot rule puts the pivot.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Hoare's original partition scheme moves two pointers inward from both ends, unlike Lomuto's single left-to-right scan. Which statement about Hoare's partition is TRUE?
options: It returns a split point that need not be the final position of the pivot.
It always leaves the pivot at its final sorted position.
It is a stable partition, so equal keys keep their relative order.
A single call of it costs Θ(n²) in the worst case.

solution.concept: Hoare's scheme guarantees only that every key left of the returned index is ≤ every key right of it; it does not isolate the pivot, so the pivot itself may move during the scan.
steps: Two pointers start at the two ends and move inward, swapping keys that are on the wrong side.
The scan stops with i ≥ j and returns j; the pivot value may have been swapped into either part along the way.
The invariant is a[lo..j] ≤ a[j+1..hi], which is enough to recurse on [lo, j] and [j+1, hi].
Lomuto, by contrast, does place the pivot at its final index, which is why its recursion excludes the pivot while Hoare's does not.
solution.final: The returned index is a split point, not the pivot's final place — option A.
solution.trap: Reading the Lomuto invariant into Hoare's code. Excluding the returned index as if it were the pivot either loses a key or loops forever on a two-element subarray.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The recursion tree of merge sort on n keys has ⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1 levels, counting the root as level 0.
Quicksort's recursion depth is Θ(log n) on average and Θ(n) in the worst case.
Heapsort runs in Θ(n log n) in the worst case and is stable.
The merge of two runs whose lengths add to m can be performed in Θ(log m) time by one processor.

solution.concept: The shape of a divide-and-conquer recursion is read off its recursion tree: the number of levels and the work per level give both the running time and the stack depth.
steps: Halving n until the pieces are of size 1 takes ⌈log₂ n⌉ splits, so the tree has ⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1 levels — (A) is true.
Quicksort recurses on both parts: balanced splits give depth Θ(log n), one-sided splits give depth Θ(n) — (B) is true.
Heapsort is Θ(n log n) in the worst case but the heap operations move keys across long distances, so it is not stable — (C) is false.
Merging has to read and write every key, which is Ω(m) work for one processor, never Θ(log m) — (D) is false.
solution.trap: Treating heapsort as stable because it is an in-place Θ(n log n) sort. Stability and asymptotic time are independent properties.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Merge sort is run on an array of n = 12 keys. How many times is the merge step executed in total? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Each call of the merge step takes two sorted runs and returns one, so a merge reduces the number of runs by exactly one.
steps: The input starts as n = 12 runs of one key each.
Every merge combines two runs into one, so the run count drops by 1 per merge.
The recursion ends with a single run, so the number of merges is 12 − 1 = 11.
This count does not depend on how evenly the array is split — only on the number of keys.
solution.trap: Counting the recursive calls instead of the merges. There are 2n − 1 calls but only n − 1 of them reach the merge step.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Quicksort's pivot always splits off exactly one element, so its comparison count obeys T(n) = T(n − 1) + (n − 1) with T(1) = 0. What is T(6)? (Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A recurrence with a linear driving function and a one-element reduction is solved by unrolling: each level costs the size of the subarray minus one.
steps: T(6) = T(5) + 5.
T(5) = T(4) + 4, T(4) = T(3) + 3, T(3) = T(2) + 2, T(2) = T(1) + 1.
Adding with T(1) = 0: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15.
In general T(n) = n(n − 1)/2, which here gives 6·5/2 = 15.
solution.trap: Substituting the size n into a closed form for the balanced case and answering n log n. The recurrence here is the one-sided one, so the answer grows quadratically.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Counting sort places each key at a position computed from the key's own value. For which input does it need a change of representation before it can be used at all?
options: Keys that are arbitrary real numbers in [0, 1)
Keys that are integers in 0 … k − 1
Keys that contain duplicates
Keys that are already in sorted order

solution.concept: Counting sort uses the key itself as an index into a count array, so the keys must be integers drawn from a small contiguous range.
steps: The count array is indexed by key value, which requires each key to be an integer in 0 … k − 1.
Real numbers in [0, 1) cannot index an array at all: there are uncountably many of them.
The usual repair is to bucket the reals into equal-width intervals and sort each bucket, which is bucket sort, not counting sort.
Duplicates and pre-sorted input are both harmless: duplicates are counted, and order is irrelevant.
