The tabulated DP is pseudo-polynomial: its running time O(nW) is polynomial in n and in the numeric value of W, but not in the number of bits used to write W.
Because 0-1 knapsack is NP-hard, no dynamic program can run in O(nW) time.
The same DP also solves the fractional knapsack problem optimally, since it examines every capacity.

solution.concept: DP applies when the problem has optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems; the O(nW) bound is a bound in the magnitude of the input numbers, not in the input size, which is what makes knapsack weakly NP-hard.
steps: Option A: if an optimal solution of (i, w) takes item i, the rest must be optimal for (i−1, w−wᵢ); otherwise replacing it with a better sub-solution improves the whole. TRUE.
Option B: W written in binary needs Θ(log W) bits, so O(nW) is exponential in the input length. TRUE.
Option C: NP-hardness concerns worst-case polynomial time in the input length; a pseudo-polynomial algorithm is entirely consistent with it. FALSE.
Option D: the fractional problem allows taking a fraction of an item, a choice the 0-1 table cannot represent; its optimum is found by sorting on value per unit weight. FALSE.
solution.trap: Believing that an O(nW) algorithm would prove P = NP. It would not, because W is part of the value of the input, not of its size.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. DP applies when the problem has optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems; the O(nW) bound is a bound in the magnitude of the input numbers, not in the input size, which is what makes knapsack weakly NP-hard.

Step by step.

  1. Option A: if an optimal solution of (i, w) takes item i, the rest must be optimal for (i−1, w−wᵢ); otherwise replacing it with a better sub-solution improves the whole. TRUE.
  2. Option B: W written in binary needs Θ(log W) bits, so O(nW) is exponential in the input length. TRUE.
  3. Option C: NP-hardness concerns worst-case polynomial time in the input length; a pseudo-polynomial algorithm is entirely consistent with it. FALSE.
  4. Option D: the fractional problem allows taking a fraction of an item, a choice the 0-1 table cannot represent; its optimum is found by sorting on value per unit weight. FALSE.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Common misconception. Believing that an O(nW) algorithm would prove P = NP. It would not, because W is part of the value of the input, not of its size.

Takeaway. Pseudo-polynomial is polynomial in values, exponential in bits.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Items are (3, 5), (4, 6) and (5, 8) as (weight, value). The knapsack has capacity W = 9 and must be filled exactly — unused capacity is not allowed. What is the maximum total value?
options: No exact filling of capacity 9 exists

solution.concept: The exact-fill variant changes the base case: K[0][0] = 0 and K[0][w] = −∞ for w > 0, so unreachable capacities stay unreachable instead of silently inheriting a smaller value.
steps: {1}: weight 3, value 5. {2}: 4, 6. {3}: 5, 8.
{1,2}: weight 7, value 11. {1,3}: 8, 13. {2,3}: 9, 14.
{1,2,3}: weight 12, exceeds the capacity.
Only {2,3} fills 9 exactly, with value 6 + 8 = 14.
solution.trap: Using the ordinary table and reporting 14 as if it came from the subset of weight 8; worse, reporting 14 for a capacity that no subset fills. Here the value happens to coincide, but the subset that attains it is the exact one.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The exact-fill variant changes the base case: K[0][0] = 0 and K[0][w] = −∞ for w > 0, so unreachable capacities stay unreachable instead of silently inheriting a smaller value.

Step by step. List the feasible subsets and their total weights:

  1. {1}: weight 3, value 5. {2}: 4, 6. {3}: 5, 8.
  2. {1,2}: weight 7, value 11. {1,3}: 8, 13. {2,3}: 9, 14.
  3. {1,2,3}: weight 12, exceeds the capacity.
  4. Only {2,3} fills 9 exactly, with value 6 + 8 = 14.

Answer: Option (C) — 14.

Common misconception. Using the ordinary table and reporting 14 as if it came from the subset of weight 8; worse, reporting 14 for a capacity that no subset fills. Here the value happens to coincide, but the subset that attains it is the exact one.

Takeaway. Exact fill needs −∞ base cases, or the answer may come from a partially filled knapsack.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Five items are given as (weight, value): (1, 2), (2, 5), (3, 7), (4, 9), (5, 11). The capacity is W = 9 and each item may be taken at most once. What is the maximum total value?(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Every item has value per unit weight between 2 and 2.5, so the greedy ratio order is a poor guide; the DP (or a full enumeration of subsets of weight at most 9) is needed.
steps: Any subset containing (1,2)+(2,5)+(3,7)+(4,9) weighs 10 and is infeasible, so the maximum over all feasible subsets is 21, attained by (2,5)+(3,7)+(4,9).
solution.trap: Assuming the ratio-greedy answer must be optimal here because it is feasible; a different subset of weight 9 could have beaten it. It has to be checked, and here it does not.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Every item has value per unit weight between 2 and 2.5, so the greedy ratio order is a poor guide; the DP (or a full enumeration of subsets of weight at most 9) is needed.

Step by step. Value per unit weight is 2, 2.5, 2.33, 2.25, 2.2, so a ratio argument is inconclusive; enumerate the best subsets by weight.

  1. Weight 9: (4,9)+(5,11) = 20; (1,2)+(3,7)+(5,11) = 20; (2,5)+(3,7)+(4,9) = 21.
  2. Weight 8: (1,2)+(3,7)+(4,9) = 18; (3,7)+(5,11) = 18; (1,2)+(2,5)+(5,11) = 18.
  3. Weight 7: (1,2)+(2,5)+(4,9) = 16; (2,5)+(5,11) = 16.
  4. Any subset containing (1,2)+(2,5)+(3,7)+(4,9) weighs 10 and is infeasible, so the maximum over all feasible subsets is 21, attained by (2,5)+(3,7)+(4,9).

Answer: 21

Common misconception. Assuming the ratio-greedy answer must be optimal here because it is feasible; a different subset of weight 9 could have beaten it. It has to be checked, and here it does not.

Takeaway. A feasible greedy answer is not a certificate of optimality.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: In the Floyd–Warshall recurrence d^(k)[i][j] = min(d^(k−1)[i][j], d^(k−1)[i][k] + d^(k−1)[k][j]), which pair of operations is used?
options: min and +
max and +
min and ×
logical OR and AND

solution.concept: Floyd–Warshall lives in the (min, +) semiring: paths are concatenated by adding their lengths and compared by taking the smaller.
steps: A path from i to j either avoids k — cost d^(k−1)[i][j] — or goes through k, cost d^(k−1)[i][k] + d^(k−1)[k][j].
Concatenating two paths adds their lengths: the +.
Choosing the better of the two options is the min.
The logical (OR, AND) pair appears in Warshall's transitive-closure algorithm, which is the reachability version of the same recurrence, not the distance version.
solution.trap: Using multiplication for concatenation, which would compute products of path lengths, or reaching for (OR, AND) when distances rather than reachability are wanted.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Floyd–Warshall lives in the (min, +) semiring: paths are concatenated by adding their lengths and compared by taking the smaller.

Step by step.

  1. A path from i to j either avoids k — cost d^(k−1)[i][j] — or goes through k, cost d^(k−1)[i][k] + d^(k−1)[k][j].
  2. Concatenating two paths adds their lengths: the +.
  3. Choosing the better of the two options is the min.
  4. The logical (OR, AND) pair appears in Warshall's transitive-closure algorithm, which is the reachability version of the same recurrence, not the distance version.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Using multiplication for concatenation, which would compute products of path lengths, or reaching for (OR, AND) when distances rather than reachability are wanted.

Takeaway. Same skeleton, two semirings: (min, +) for distances, (OR, AND) for reachability.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: A directed graph has vertices A, B, C, D and weighted edges A→B (3), B→C (4), A→C (10) and C→D (2). What distance does Floyd–Warshall report for the pair (A, D)?(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Floyd–Warshall ends with the true shortest-path distance between every pair, so the answer is the cost of the cheapest walk from A to D.
steps: The only route into D is C→D, so every walk to D goes through C and costs d(A, C) + 2.
Two ways reach C: direct A→C = 10, or A→B→C = 3 + 4 = 7.
So d(A, C) = 7 and d(A, D) = 7 + 2 = 9.
The intermediate vertex B is discovered in iteration k = B, which lowers d[A][C] from 10 to 7; iteration k = C then lowers d[A][D] from ∞ to 9.
solution.trap: Following the single path the eye finds first (A→C→D = 12) instead of comparing the two routes into C.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Floyd–Warshall ends with the true shortest-path distance between every pair, so the answer is the cost of the cheapest walk from A to D.

Step by step.

  1. The only route into D is C→D, so every walk to D goes through C and costs d(A, C) + 2.
  2. Two ways reach C: direct A→C = 10, or A→B→C = 3 + 4 = 7.
  3. So d(A, C) = 7 and d(A, D) = 7 + 2 = 9.
  4. The intermediate vertex B is discovered in iteration k = B, which lowers d[A][C] from 10 to 7; iteration k = C then lowers d[A][D] from ∞ to 9.

Answer: 9

Common misconception. Following the single path the eye finds first (A→C→D = 12) instead of comparing the two routes into C.

Takeaway. Subpaths of shortest paths are shortest: solve d(A, C) first.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: A directed graph with no negative cycle contains exactly one edge of negative weight. Which statement is TRUE?
options: Dijkstra's algorithm still returns correct distances, because the graph is connected.
Floyd–Warshall returns correct all-pairs distances, because it needs only the absence of negative cycles.
Floyd–Warshall fails, because the initial distance matrix contains a negative entry.
No all-pairs algorithm can be applied until the negative edge is removed or the weights are reweighted.

solution.concept: Floyd–Warshall's correctness depends on the optimal substructure of shortest paths, which holds whenever no negative cycle is reachable; it never relies on a greedy choice, so negative edges are harmless.
steps: Dijkstra's invariant — the closest unsettled vertex can be settled — breaks as soon as a negative edge can shorten a path through an unsettled vertex, so option (A) is FALSE.
Floyd–Warshall examines every intermediate vertex in every order of length, so a negative edge is just another candidate term; with no negative cycle the minimum is attained by a simple path. TRUE.
A negative initial entry is not an error condition: it is an edge weight. FALSE for (C).
Reweighting (Johnson) is one way to use Dijkstra on all pairs, not a precondition for Floyd–Warshall. FALSE for (D).
solution.trap: Treating ‘non-negative weights’ as a requirement of Floyd–Warshall. It is a requirement of Dijkstra, and of Johnson's reweighting step only in the sense that the result must be non-negative.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Floyd–Warshall's correctness depends on the optimal substructure of shortest paths, which holds whenever no negative cycle is reachable; it never relies on a greedy choice, so negative edges are harmless.

Step by step.

  1. Dijkstra's invariant — the closest unsettled vertex can be settled — breaks as soon as a negative edge can shorten a path through an unsettled vertex, so option (A) is FALSE.
  2. Floyd–Warshall examines every intermediate vertex in every order of length, so a negative edge is just another candidate term; with no negative cycle the minimum is attained by a simple path. TRUE.
  3. A negative initial entry is not an error condition: it is an edge weight. FALSE for (C).
  4. Reweighting (Johnson) is one way to use Dijkstra on all pairs, not a precondition for Floyd–Warshall. FALSE for (D).

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Treating ‘non-negative weights’ as a requirement of Floyd–Warshall. It is a requirement of Dijkstra, and of Johnson's reweighting step only in the sense that the result must be non-negative.

Takeaway. Negative edges are fine for all-pairs DP; negative cycles are not.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following statements about Floyd–Warshall and transitive closure are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Warshall's transitive-closure algorithm replaces min by logical OR and + by logical AND in the same three-loop skeleton.
Transitive closure can be computed by repeated squaring of the boolean adjacency matrix, in O(V³ log V) time.
After the algorithm has run, a negative cycle is present if and only if some diagonal entry d[i][i] is negative.
The algorithm requires the graph to be strongly connected, otherwise unreachable pairs are reported as distance 0.

solution.concept: The triple loop computes a closure in any semiring; over the booleans it gives reachability, and the diagonal of the distance version exposes negative cycles.
steps: Option A: reachability composes by AND along a path and combines alternatives by OR, exactly mirroring + and min. TRUE.
Option B: squaring the boolean matrix ⌈log₂ V⌉ times gives paths of length up to V−1, each product costing O(V³) with ordinary matrix multiplication. TRUE.
Option C: d[i][i] is the cheapest cycle through i; it starts at 0 and is negative only if a negative cycle is reachable from and returns to i. TRUE.
Option D: unreachable pairs stay at ∞, never 0; connectivity is not required. FALSE.
solution.trap: Thinking a negative diagonal entry means d[i][i] was initialised wrongly. The initialisation is 0; a negative value is the detection signal.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The triple loop computes a closure in any semiring; over the booleans it gives reachability, and the diagonal of the distance version exposes negative cycles.

Step by step.

  1. Option A: reachability composes by AND along a path and combines alternatives by OR, exactly mirroring + and min. TRUE.
  2. Option B: squaring the boolean matrix ⌈log₂ V⌉ times gives paths of length up to V−1, each product costing O(V³) with ordinary matrix multiplication. TRUE.
  3. Option C: d[i][i] is the cheapest cycle through i; it starts at 0 and is negative only if a negative cycle is reachable from and returns to i. TRUE.
  4. Option D: unreachable pairs stay at ∞, never 0; connectivity is not required. FALSE.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Thinking a negative diagonal entry means d[i][i] was initialised wrongly. The initialisation is 0; a negative value is the detection signal.

Takeaway. Check the diagonal after the run to certify the absence of negative cycles.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: A directed graph has vertices 1, 2, 3, 4 and edges 1→2 (2), 2→3 (−5), 3→2 (1) and 3→4 (1). The matrix is initialised with d[i][i] = 0 and ∞ where no edge exists, and Floyd–Warshall is run to completion, reporting −∞ wherever the distance is unbounded below. How many ordered pairs (u, v), including those with u = v, have d[u][v] = −∞?

solution.concept: d[u][v] = −∞ exactly when u can reach a negative cycle and v is reachable from that cycle: then a walk can loop the cycle arbitrarily often before continuing.
steps: Find the cycle: 2→3→2 has weight −5 + 1 = −4 < 0, so it is a negative cycle.
Which vertices reach it? 1 (via 1→2), 2 and 3 (both on the cycle). So u ∈ {1, 2, 3}.
Which vertices are reachable from it? 2, 3 on the cycle and 4 via 3→4. So v ∈ {2, 3, 4}.
Every combination gives an unbounded-below distance: 3 × 3 = 9 pairs. For example d[1][4] loops the cycle and then exits through 3→4, so it can be made as small as desired.
Pairs involving vertex 1 as a destination, or vertex 4 as a source, stay finite (or ∞), so the count is exactly 9.
solution.trap: Counting only the cycle's own vertices (the 4 pairs inside {2,3}), which ignores every pair that merely passes through the cycle.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. d[u][v] = −∞ exactly when u can reach a negative cycle and v is reachable from that cycle: then a walk can loop the cycle arbitrarily often before continuing.

Step by step.

  1. Find the cycle: 2→3→2 has weight −5 + 1 = −4 < 0, so it is a negative cycle.
  2. Which vertices reach it? 1 (via 1→2), 2 and 3 (both on the cycle). So u ∈ {1, 2, 3}.
  3. Which vertices are reachable from it? 2, 3 on the cycle and 4 via 3→4. So v ∈ {2, 3, 4}.
  4. Every combination gives an unbounded-below distance: 3 × 3 = 9 pairs. For example d[1][4] loops the cycle and then exits through 3→4, so it can be made as small as desired.
  5. Pairs involving vertex 1 as a destination, or vertex 4 as a source, stay finite (or ∞), so the count is exactly 9.

Answer: Option (C) — 9 pairs.

Common misconception. Counting only the cycle's own vertices (the 4 pairs inside {2,3}), which ignores every pair that merely passes through the cycle.

Takeaway. Unboundedness spreads to reach-in × reach-out, not to the cycle alone.

questions.subject: algorithms
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the Floyd–Warshall algorithm are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Its running time is Θ(V³) for V vertices, independent of the number of edges.
It computes correct all-pairs distances with negative edge weights provided no negative cycle is reachable.
It requires every edge weight to be non-negative.
Its initial matrix d^(0) holds the edge weight where an edge exists, ∞ where none exists, and 0 on the diagonal.

solution.concept: Floyd–Warshall is a three-level DP over intermediate vertices: one loop per vertex over all V² pairs, so the work is fixed by the vertex count and the correctness condition is the absence of negative cycles.
steps: Option A: the loops run V, V and V times with constant work inside, so Θ(V³) whatever the edge density. TRUE.
Option B: each iteration only compares candidate sums, which stays valid while shortest paths are well defined. TRUE.
Option C: negative edges are accepted; only negative cycles break correctness. FALSE.
Option D: that initialisation encodes one-edge paths and the empty path. TRUE.
solution.trap: Confusing the non-negativity requirement of Dijkstra with a requirement of Floyd–Warshall, and so refusing to use it on graphs with negative edges.

Detailed solution

Concept. Floyd–Warshall is a three-level DP over intermediate vertices: one loop per vertex over all V² pairs, so the work is fixed by the vertex count and the correctness condition is the absence of negative cycles.

Step by step.

  1. Option A: the loops run V, V and V times with constant work inside, so Θ(V³) whatever the edge density. TRUE.
  2. Option B: each iteration only compares candidate sums, which stays valid while shortest paths are well defined. TRUE.

Common misconception. Confusing the non-negativity requirement of Dijkstra with a requirement of Floyd–Warshall, and so refusing to use it on graphs with negative edges.
